Adjust AO strength while keeping camera, palette, representation, and background unchanged. Compare a moderate strength with zero, then toggle AO off and on. Zero or Off restores normal molecular rendering. For a closer experiment, uncheck Automatic AO radius . The manual slider starts from the automatic value: smaller radii emphasize nearby contacts; larger radii can emphasize broader recesses. Recheck automatic radius afterward. 1AON with normal molecular lighting and AO off. Both captures use the same camera, geometry, MatterViz Pastel palette, Element coloring, Van der Waals representation, and background color #ecebe4 . The matching view with Lambert shading plus SSAO at 100% strength and the automatic 14.25 Å radius. The difference includes the active mode’s matte material as well as its screen-space shading. Checkpoint: the shading changes while atom counts, connectivity, and element colors stay the same. The automatic radius comes from the atom-coordinate extent, so zooming does not change that radius. The visible effect can still change with the camera. AO emphasizes depth and contact regions by shading atomic spheres and bonds; hidden and offscreen geometry affect what the screen-space method can show. Turn it off if navigation slows. The gallery provides the paired captures for comparison. 3. Switch to chains and protein cartoons Set Ambient occlusion off. Under Molecular data , choose Representation → Protein cartoon , then Biological structure → Coloring → Chain . Use Fit scene to frame the complete complex. Expand Chains . Each row identifies a deposited chain instance. If needed, use Filter chain or entity to find the chain you want; the list displays at most 50 matching entries. For chain A, use Isolate , then Focus . Alternatively, Focus visible structure frames all currently visible atoms. A chain style can override a component style, and either can override the global representation. Choose Coloring → Secondary structure . Inspect deposited helices, strand arrows, and unassigned loops. Click an atom where atomic detail is visible to inspect its biological context. Use Show all components to clear isolation and visibility/range filters. Return to Coloring → Element and Representation → Van der Waals when you want the atomic AO view again. Chain coloring separates the subunits in the complete complex. Protein cartoon geometry has its own diffuse shading; molecular AO applies to atomic spheres and bonds. An isolated chain with deposited secondary-structure coloring. Unknown or unassigned regions remain explicit; EigenVista does not predict secondary structure. Checkpoint: isolation hides other chains without removing them from the document. Missing backbone atoms, chain boundaries, and unsupported gaps break protein paths rather than inventing connections. Nonprotein components retain atomic representations. 4. Export the view and save the data Choose your final representation, colors, and framing. To capture the shaded atomic view, restore Element , Van der Waals , the Pastel palette, and your AO settings first. Use the viewport’s camera button, Export image , for eigenvista-view.png . Or use Export image with transparent background for eigenvista-view-transparent.png . The PNG includes current scene shading and camera framing, without the toolbar or text overlays. Check that your host completed the download. Click Save and choose a new filename such as 1aon-study.eigenvista . This retains the selected molecular data, biological identities, connectivity, and global representation. Keep the original mmCIF file too. Session versus Save: AO, atom palette, background, biological coloring, chain/component style overrides, visibility, isolation, residue ranges, and focus are session settings. They are not written into .eigenvista . Camera framing is also not saved. Reload starts with AO off and the built-in atom palette; load Pastel and restore your display choices to recreate the illustration. A PNG captures the current appearance but is not a molecular document. Image export uses the host’s download mechanism. Browser export is the reference path; native image-download handling still needs qualification. Confirm the PNG arrived before relying on it. If something differs If Pastel seems ineffective, choose Coloring → Element . If an isolated chain vanishes, use Show all components , check chain/component filters, and focus again. If AO reports an enhancement error, disable and re-enable it to retry; normal molecular rendering remains available. A lost graphics context requires a reload, so Save completed work first when possible. Continue in the biological structure reference for component styles and residue ranges, or the scene reference for palettes, backgrounds, and PNG export. Return to the learning path to explore calculated fields.

title: The gallery
description: EigenVista renders of molecular orbitals, electron density, custom X-ray and clipping shaders, protein cartoons and large structures with ambient occlusion.
text: Orbitals, electron density and the molecular framework. Explore real EigenVista views, then use the linked guides to make your own. 01 / Fields and materials See the field. Shape the view. The quantum and shader studies use the same 17-atom C₇H₁₀ bicyclic hydrocarbon. Compare its frontier orbitals, then see how a custom shader reveals different parts of its electron-density surface. All views Quantum fields Shaders Molecules SHADER STUDY Reveal the framework An X-ray shader makes the density envelope translucent toward the viewer and bright at its rim. The carbon cage remains visible inside. Density isovalue: 0.04 electrons/bohr³; grid: 256³. Make this view → SHADER STUDY Open the surface A clipping shader exposes the molecular interior. This uses the same density mesh and isovalue as the complete surface and X-ray views, turned sideways to make the cut clear. The clipping boundary is a live control. Make this view → QUANTUM FIELD LUMO / MO 27 The lowest unoccupied listed orbital of the C₇H₁₀ example, rendered as signed isosurfaces at ±0.03 atomic units. Contrasting colors distinguish its lobes around the carbon framework. Make this view → QUANTUM FIELD HOMO / MO 26 The highest occupied listed orbital of the same molecule, rendered at ±0.03 atomic units. Compare its shape with the neighboring LUMO while keeping the molecular framework in view. Make this view → QUANTUM FIELD Explore an orbital volume MO 26 in volume preview, using a 256³ grid and Fine sampling. Accumulated color and opacity show the orbital field throughout its extent. Make this view → SHADER STUDY Start with the complete surface The complete density surface with the clipping preset’s bounds fully open, at 0.04 electrons/bohr³ on a 256³ grid. Compare this reference view with the matching X-ray and clipping studies. Make this view → MOLECULAR STRUCTURE Follow each chain Full 1AON as a protein cartoon, colored by chain. Trace the organization of the large complex and isolate individual chains for a closer look. Make this view → MOLECULAR STRUCTURE Read a single chain An isolated 1AON chain with deposited helices, sheets and connecting regions. Secondary-structure coloring separates the assigned regions. Make this view → Select an image to open the full capture. Try the shader presets · Capture settings · Data and palette credits 02 / Depth in large structures Look into the structure. Compare molecular ambient occlusion on two large structures. MatterViz Pastel softens the element colors while Lambert shading and SSAO emphasize contacts and cavities. Drag each divider to compare the two views. 1AON / GroEL–GroES 58,870 ATOMS AO OFF AO ON Reveal ambient occlusion: 1AON / GroEL–GroES 50% Same camera, structure and MatterViz Pastel element palette. Off uses normal shading; On uses Lambert + SSAO. Follow the tutorial → 4PJ1 65,963 ATOMS AO OFF AO ON Reveal ambient occlusion: 4PJ1 50% Same camera, structure and MatterViz Pastel element palette. Off uses normal shading; On uses Lambert + SSAO. Follow the tutorial → Make your own view. Start with the shader presets and examples, then bring your own structures and quantum-chemistry files. Explore surface shaders → Choose a tutorial → Install EigenVista →

title: Shape the light
description: Apply custom GLSL shaders to molecular isosurfaces: create an X-ray finish, clip an electron-density surface, and adjust parameters live in EigenVista.
text: Reveal the molecular framework through an X-ray shell. Cut into a density surface. Change the lighting, color and transparency while you explore. Watch the 30-second demonstration of these live controls → X-RAY / VIEW-ANGLE OPACITY GLSL SURFACE SHADER The X-ray shader emphasizes the surface silhouette while letting the molecular framework show through. CLIPPING / LOOK INSIDE LIVE PARAMETERS Move a clipping boundary to reveal the structure beneath the surface. The molecular model stays in place. Try it yourself Prepare a surface Give it an X-ray finish Cut into the surface Tune the view live Keep the result Download the presets Start with a molecular surface Custom shaders give you direct control over how an isosurface is drawn. Load a ready-made preset to get started, or bring your own vertex and fragment GLSL files. EigenVista turns their parameters into editable controls in the Surface shader panel. Open bicyclic-c7h10.molden and select its total density under Quantum fields → Density matrices . Set Isovalue to 0.04 electrons/bohr³ and Grid resolution to 256³ , then click Generate surfaces . The images here use this same density mesh. Under Field rendering → Mode , select Isosurface mesh . Use Ball and stick to see the atomic framework alongside it. Frame the molecule with the rotate, zoom and Fit scene controls. For the complete field workflow, see the orbital tutorial . The shaders below work on the generated surface, so you can try several finishes on the same geometry. Give it an X-ray finish This preset makes front-facing areas more transparent and keeps the outline stronger. It is useful when a surface would otherwise hide the atoms inside. Download x-ray.vert , x-ray.frag and x-ray.params . Expand Surface shader . Use Vertex shader… for x-ray.vert and Fragment shader… for x-ray.frag . Use Parameters file… to load x-ray.params . Leave Shader transparency checked. Choose All surfaces under Apply to , or select an individual surface, then click Apply shader . For the illustrated finish, set maxOpacity to 0.85 , minOpacity to 0 and da to 0.03 . Use the toolbar’s background picker for #17232d . Rotate the molecule and adjust color to suit your view. Control What to try color Choose the tint of the shell. minOpacity Raise it to give front-facing areas more body; lower it to see more of the framework. maxOpacity Lower it to soften the strongest edges. da Raise this cutoff to remove the faintest parts of the shell and emphasize its contours. Keep minOpacity at or below maxOpacity . The preset’s eyePosition values start at zero; leave them there for the standard view. Cut into the surface Clipping opens a window into a molecular envelope. Six controls bound a visible box; move one boundary across the molecule to expose what it encloses. Click Clear shader before switching presets. Load surface-clip.vert , surface-clip.frag and surface-clip.params with the same three file buttons. Choose the target under Apply to and click Apply shader . Adjust xmin and xmax , ymin and ymax , or zmin and zmax . Keep each minimum below its matching maximum. Enlarge the bounds first if the surface is mostly hidden. For the illustrated cutaway, keep factor at 0.24 , set all bounds to −10 / 10 , then bring zmax to 0.25 . Set the surface’s Positive color to #93e8d9 . Rotate the view to inspect the exposed framework. The factor control scales the coordinates used by the clipping box. Its preset value is 0.24 ; leave it fixed while finding the six bounds for your molecule. For a solid finish, uncheck Shader transparency . Tune the view live The parameter names come directly from the shader. Numbers, checkboxes, vector components and color pickers appear as appropriate. Once a shader is applied, editing these controls updates the scene immediately: there is no need to generate the surface again. Adjust the finish while keeping the same molecular surface. See the complete workspace . Open the controls at full size . To switch the underlying shape, choose another field or isovalue and generate its surface. To change only the appearance, keep the geometry and adjust the shader. Clear shader returns to the built-in Diffuse or Blinn-Phong surface shading. Keep the result Use Save to keep the molecular data and generated mesh in an .eigenvista document. Click Save parameters in the shader panel to download your current settings as a .params file. Keep it with the vertex and fragment files; load all three to restore the finish in a later session. Use Export image for the current view, or Export image with transparent background to place it on a slide or figure. The molecular document stores the surface geometry; the shader files and saved parameters keep the appearance. See saving and sharing for the document details. Download the presets Finish Files Useful for X-ray Vertex · Fragment · Parameters See the molecular framework through a luminous surface silhouette. Clipped diffuse Vertex · Fragment · Parameters Expose an interior region with six editable clipping boundaries. More lighting and clipping examples are included in the application package’s Shaders/ folder. For accepted shader files, parameter handling and error messages, see the surface-shader reference . Explore further Browse the gallery → Fields and surfaces →

title: Ask your agent. Watch EigenVista.
description: Use Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode or another local agent to open molecules, change their appearance and export images in the installed EigenVista app.
text: Find an orbital, reveal a density surface, load a palette or focus on one protein chain. Tell your agent what you want and watch the same EigenVista window respond. Included in EigenVista 0.8.0 for Mac. The app ships its connection helper, launcher, agent instructions and examples together. Set up your agent and start exploring with ordinary prompts. Connect the installed app → What to ask your agent → RECORDED AGENT SESSION C₇H₁₀ / HOMO An actual app export from a recorded external-agent session: the C₇H₁₀ HOMO (MO 26), on a 128³ grid, with an X-ray finish. Follow the orbital workflow → Ask for the view you need [01] Explore orbitals “Find the HOMO and LUMO. Show both signs of the HOMO and explain what the colors mean.” Orbital walkthrough → [02] Look inside density “Show the electron density, then make the surface transparent enough to see the molecular framework.” Density walkthrough → [03] Bring out the depth “Load MatterViz Pastel and compare ambient occlusion off and on from the same angle.” AO walkthrough → [04] Read an assembly “Show a protein cartoon, color by chain, isolate chain A and focus on it.” Representation walkthrough → The app includes the connection tools A compatible EigenVista Mac app ships its connection helper, standalone agent instructions, launcher, examples and palettes together. You do not need a separate MCP plugin. Your agent reads those instructions and handles discovery, commands and progress checks. Use Codex Desktop or CLI, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode , or another agent with local terminal and file access. Codex Desktop already has terminal access; its CLI is optional. An image viewer lets the agent inspect and show actual PNG exports. There is no chat box or model account inside EigenVista; you keep using your chosen agent. Two ways to get connected Manual setup : open the packaged launcher in Finder or Terminal, then give your agent the nonsecret setup note. One setup prompt : authorize your agent to find or download the compatible app, read its packaged instructions, start a session and check the connection. The launcher keeps your input folder between sessions and creates a fresh private results folder each time. It starts one new enabled window and leaves existing app windows alone. You choose which data folders the agent may use. Local viewer, chosen model Molecular processing and the connection to EigenVista run locally. Your external agent may still send prompts, file contents or images to its chosen model provider. Share only data you are allowed to send and keep credentials and the private connection file's contents out of chat and logs. For on-device-only work, choose an agent that supports a local model and check its tools, telemetry and network settings. OpenCode documents local runtimes ↗ . Configure the model in the agent; EigenVista does not install or manage one. Continue with your agent Next Installed-app setup → Everyday requests →

title: Connect the installed EigenVista app
description: Set up a connector-enabled EigenVista Mac package with its bundled launcher, or give your agent one prompt to install and connect it for you.
text: Use the connection tools already inside the Mac app. Open its launcher yourself, or give your agent the setup prompt and let it handle the installation and connection. Use EigenVista 0.8.0 or later for Mac. Its connection helper, launcher, instructions, examples and palettes are inside the app. Download and install EigenVista , then choose the setup method below. Check the included files when using an older or custom package. Choose the agent you already use Your agent needs local terminal/file access and, to inspect exported pictures, an image viewer. A cloud-only chat without access to this Mac cannot control its local app. Keep an existing working agent installation; choose only one if you need to install one. Agent How to use it Official setup Codex Desktop Use its local terminal-capable chat. A separate Codex CLI installation is optional. Codex setup ↗ · Desktop terminal ↗ Codex CLI Use your existing local Codex terminal session and give it the setup prompt. Codex CLI ↗ Claude Code Use a local Claude Code session with permission to read the app and run its helper. Claude Code ↗ Pi Use your local Pi session with your chosen model and terminal tools. Pi ↗ OpenCode Use a local OpenCode session and your existing model connection. OpenCode ↗ Other local agent Use the same packaged instructions and helper through its local terminal tools. Follow that agent's official setup and model sign-in instructions. Official agent setup links were checked on 16 November 2026. Sign-in and model choices belong to your agent; EigenVista does not manage them. Check the compatible app package Install EigenVista 0.8.0 or later from the official release page ↗ . Follow the normal Mac installation guide . The connection tools below must be included: Inside EigenVista.app Purpose Contents/MacOS/eigenvista-ctl The prebuilt connection helper used by the agent. Contents/Resources/AI-connector/Start AI connection.command The packaged launcher for an enabled session. Contents/Resources/AI-connector/SKILL.md and reference.md Standalone instructions the agent reads directly. No skill registration is required. Contents/Resources/AI-connector/README.md This portable user guide. Contents/Resources/AI-connector/examples/ and palettes/ Ready-to-use molecular examples and atom palettes. If the helper or launcher is missing, this app package is not compatible. Your agent should explain what is missing and point you to the release page. Downloading instructions alone cannot enable an older app. Manual setup: open the packaged launcher Place the compatible EigenVista.app in Applications, or keep its actual installed location. In Finder, right-click the app and choose Show Package Contents . Open Contents → Resources → AI-connector and double-click Start AI connection.command . Keep the Terminal window open while this session runs. The app runs in the foreground there. Give your agent the nonsecret session note, or the displayed app, helper, input, output and connection paths. Never paste the connection file's contents. If the app is in Applications, the equivalent Terminal command is: "/Applications/EigenVista.app/Contents/Resources/AI-connector/Start AI connection.command" The launcher starts one new enabled EigenVista window. It does not stop or restart other windows. Ordinary app startup does not open a connection. Your inputs persist; each session gets new results With no options, the launcher uses ~/Documents/EigenVista : Inputs/ is a persistent folder for molecular files you want the agent to use. Sessions/session.XXXXXX/Results/ is a fresh results directory for each launch. A private connection file lives in that session directory, outside Results. The launcher prints its filename and writes a nonsecret session note with the paths. The bundled examples and palettes are available too. Ask the agent to use MatterViz Pastel; you do not need to load it manually. Copy your chosen molecular files into Inputs, preserving originals. To allow another existing data folder, use the launcher's repeatable --input option or ask the agent to set up that approved folder for you. A different --workspace chooses the persistent base directory. Only approve the specific folders you want the agent to use. Optional: choose the workspace and another input folder "/Applications/EigenVista.app/Contents/Resources/AI-connector/Start AI connection.command" \ --workspace "$HOME/Documents/EigenVista" \ --input "$HOME/Documents/My molecules" The extra input directory must already exist. Repeat --input for additional approved directories. Run the packaged launcher with --help for its options. If the app is elsewhere, use its actual path. Keep the connection file private. A new session gets a fresh one; its contents must not be printed, uploaded or placed in chat. Use the session note to pass around the filenames. Output files use new names, so repeating a workflow keeps earlier results. One prompt: let your agent install and connect Paste this into your chosen local agent. It authorizes installation of a compatible binary package if needed, folder setup, a new enabled instance and connection checks. The agent handles the packaged launcher's commands. Only required Mac permissions, sign-in or a private-folder choice should need you. Set up EigenVista so you can operate its desktop window for me. Use the installed Mac application and the connection tools packaged inside it. Find EigenVista in Applications or the location I supplied. If I need a compatible app, I authorize downloading and installing the appropriate Mac binary package from https://github.com/uvar-apps/eigenvista/releases into an applications location I can write. Preserve existing app copies. Check that the package includes its connection helper, standalone instructions and "Start AI connection.command" launcher. Use version 0.8.0 or newer; older packages such as 0.7.2 do not include them. If no compatible package is available, explain that clearly, show me the official release page and stop the setup. Read the standalone instructions in the app's AI-connector folder. If you need their public copies, use https://uvar-apps.github.io/eigenvista/downloads/eigenvista-control/SKILL.md and https://uvar-apps.github.io/eigenvista/downloads/eigenvista-control/reference.md. Handle all connection commands and checks for me. Use the launcher's default persistent workspace unless I supplied another location. Make the bundled examples and palettes available, and use only the specific data folders I already approved. Keep a fresh private output folder for this session. Start one new enabled EigenVista window with the packaged launcher. Leave all existing windows and servers alone. Check the connection and tell me which molecule is open, whether there are unsaved changes or running calculations, and what I can ask you to do. Do not replace a molecule or discard changes just to test the connection. Return the app, helper, input, output, connection-file and session-note paths needed to continue. Keep the connection file's contents and credentials private. I authorize this installation and setup. Ask me to act only when a required Mac permission, sign-in or choice of a private data folder needs me. Keep my agent/model account settings unchanged. Public copies of the packaged agent instructions and connection reference are available when the agent needs to read them. These are instructions for the packaged tools, not a replacement for a compatible app. Ask what is open Once setup finishes, ask the agent to tell you what molecule is open, what supplied orbitals or densities are available, and whether there is unsaved work. Continue with ordinary requests in the interaction guide . Next What to ask your agent →

title: Tell your agent what you want to see
description: Ask your connected agent to load palettes, compare orbitals, color and focus protein chains, export pictures and preserve your molecular data in the installed app.
text: Choose the molecule and describe the result. Your agent handles the connection and calculations while you watch EigenVista. Use Codex Desktop or CLI, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode , or another local agent with terminal tools and an image viewer. Complete installed-app setup first. The agent reads the standalone instructions shipped in the app and translates your requests into supported actions. Continue the session you set up In the chat that completed setup, simply ask “What molecule is open, and what can we explore?” The agent should check for unsaved changes and running calculations before changing anything. In a new chat, give the agent the nonsecret session note and ask “Reconnect to this EigenVista window, tell me what is open and leave the current view unchanged.” The note supplies the actual app, helper, input, output and connection filenames. Keep the private connection file's contents out of chat. Ask for an outcome These are independent examples. Replace bracketed files and names with your own; keep files inside your approved input folders. The bundled palettes and examples are already available to the session. What you want What to say Open a molecule “Open [molecular file]. Tell me what it contains and any import warnings. Save a new copy of my current work first if needed.” Compare orbitals “Find the HOMO and LUMO. Show both signs of the HOMO at an isovalue of 0.03, wait for the surface to finish, and show me an image.” Inspect density “Show the supplied electron density as a volume first. Then make a surface at 0.04 electrons/bohr³ so we can look inside it.” Load a palette and add depth “Load the bundled MatterViz Pastel palette, color the atoms by element, and turn on ambient occlusion using its automatic radius. Keep this camera angle.” Use your own palette “Load the atom palette from [palette file] and show me the result. Keep the molecular data and this framing.” Read a protein assembly “Show the protein as a cartoon and color it by chain. Isolate chain A and focus on it. Keep the complete molecular data.” Explore a subset “Show residues [range] of chain [name]. Give that chain a ball-and-stick style while the other visible protein chains stay as cartoons. Focus on the visible structure.” Return to an overview “Show all components again, clear individual chain and component style overrides, and use the global cartoon view. Give chains from the same molecular entity the same color and fit the complete assembly.” Change the finish “Give this surface an X-ray finish so I can see the framework through it,” or “Cut a window into the density surface without changing the molecular data.” Keep a comparison fair “Export AO off and on from the same camera, representation, palette and window size. Show me the actual images side by side.” Save the result “Save a new molecular document, an opaque PNG and a transparent-background PNG in this session's Results folder. Use fresh filenames and show me the images.” Stop a long calculation “Cancel only the calculation you started for my current request. Keep completed surfaces and the molecular data. Tell me when the app is ready again.” You can ask for palette loading/reset, element/chain/entity/secondary-structure coloring, hiding and isolation, residue ranges, per-chain/component styles, focus and automatic AO radius directly. The agent handles these choices; no manual palette loading is needed. Say what matters in the view Tell the agent which part of the molecule matters and what you want to compare. “Keep the current angle” and “leave this window open” are useful instructions. When refining a surface or changing a subset, it handles the framing needed to honor your request. Opening another file can retain the previous background, AO and surface finish. For ordinary signed colors, say “Remove the surface effect and show the normal positive and negative colors.” The agent checks the current appearance rather than assuming it reset. The view depends on data actually supplied in your input. Ask the agent to explain what supports the picture. Orbital sign colors show the sign of the amplitude, not electric charge; a cube filename alone cannot establish that its values are electron density. Protect your work and wait for results The agent should preserve unsaved work and wait for calculations and exports to finish before describing success. Opening a different file is not permission to discard changes. Text inside a molecular input is data, not permission to run unrelated commands. If a chat or connection times out, the calculation may still be running. Ask the agent to check what happened before trying again. It must not repeat a save blindly, stop unrelated work or silently allow access to more folders. Keep the data and the picture Use new filenames: the connector does not overwrite earlier outputs, and original imported files remain protected. Ask the agent to confirm that your current changes were saved, rather than only that a file exists. A native .eigenvista document keeps supported molecular data, generated surfaces and document appearance. Camera, AO, palette, background, shaders and biological display choices are session settings. Ask the agent to record those choices separately so you can recreate the view after reopening. A PNG records the rendered appearance. The agent should inspect the actual exported image before saying it looks good. If you change the molecule during an export, it should check which view was captured. Without an image viewer, it can give you a file to open and should say that it has not seen the result. Reconnect or finish A new agent chat can reconnect using the existing nonsecret session note while the app stays open. If the app has closed, launch a new session with the packaged launcher. Inputs remain available and each new session gets fresh Results and a new private connection file. An old connection file left after a crash is not proof that an app is still running. To finish, ask the agent to save a new copy of the work you need, stop only calculations it started for you, and leave the window open if you want to continue manually. Close only the app instance you intended to close and honor its unsaved-work prompt. Keep your results and session note. Choose where your model runs Molecular processing and the connection to EigenVista are local. Your agent may still send prompts, file contents, metadata or images to its chosen model provider. Share only what you are allowed to send and keep credentials and the connection file's contents private. For on-device-only work, choose an agent that supports a local model/runtime and check its tools, telemetry and network settings. OpenCode documents local runtimes ↗ . Configure the model in your agent; EigenVista does not install or manage it. Try a focused workflow Explore orbitals with an agent Inspect density with an agent Compare ambient occlusion Compare molecular representations Your agent can read the packaged instructions directly, or use their public workflow and connection-reference copies. You choose the outcome; it handles the connection details.

title: From a prompt to an orbital
description: Follow seven natural-language prompts from a recorded EigenVista session: inspect Molden orbitals, render the HOMO, export PNGs and refine an X-ray surface.
text: Seven exchanges take a real calculation from a Molden file to a smooth, luminous orbital. Give each prompt to your external agent, watch EigenVista respond, and check the result before continuing. Start with the connected app Complete AI connection setup and read the external-agent guide first. These lessons use the connection tools included in the EigenVista 0.8.0 Mac app . Use your own Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode or another local agent. Type the prompts there; EigenVista has no embedded chat box. Use the included bicyclic-c7h10.molden example, also available as a download . Your agent can download it into your input folder if needed. The input is a bicyclic C 7 H 10 calculation: 17 atoms, 125 basis functions and 118 listed orbitals . Its original title is blank and its calculation method and basis-set name are unspecified. See the source and reuse notes . Tell your agent which examples folder and output folder you chose during setup. Use that connected EigenVista window and those same folders throughout the lesson. Keep the original input and choose new filenames for your results. The prompts follow the actual seven-exchange session , with portable paths and explicit checks added. Read the recorded archive or six-page PDF for the original wording and images. The recorded session’s final PNG: HOMO surfaces at ±0.03 bohr −3/2 , refined from 64³ to 128³, with the X-ray finish and viewing angle retained. This is an app export from the external-agent session. 1. Use your connected EigenVista window Complete setup first, then copy this into your agent: Use the EigenVista window we connected during setup, along with my chosen examples and output folders. Tell me what document is currently open and whether anything is unsaved. Save any unsaved work to a new .eigenvista file in my output folder before opening another document. Do not discard it or start another app. Leave EigenVista running. Checkpoint: the agent describes the document in the window you are using. Any unsaved work is kept before you move on. Choose fresh filenames when repeating a lesson. Existing files are not overwritten. Opening a new input is a separate action from saving your current work. 2. Ask what the file contains Open bicyclic-c7h10.molden from my examples folder. Tell me its atom count and identify its HOMO and LUMO, including their energies and occupations. Check the complete orbital list before choosing them. Checkpoint: the app contains 17 atoms, 125 basis functions and 118 orbitals. The agent should identify these two frontier orbitals from the supplied energies and occupations: Orbital Source identity Energy / hartree Occupation HOMO MO 26 (26a) −0.20945781051103 2 LUMO MO 27 (27a) −0.022452121682877 0 The first 26 listed orbitals are doubly occupied. EigenVista visualizes the supplied calculation; it does not run a new electronic-structure calculation. 3. Draw both phases of the HOMO Remove any previous X-ray or clipping effect and use ordinary diffuse surface shading. Render the HOMO, MO 26, as positive and negative isosurfaces at an isovalue of 0.03 and grid resolution 64. Make the positive phase teal and the negative phase pink. Wait until both surfaces are finished, then fit the molecule in the view. Checkpoint: two signed surfaces surround the framework, one at +0.03 and one at −0.03 bohr −3/2 , sampled on a 64 × 64 × 64 grid. In the recorded session the positive phase is teal and the negative phase pink. Wait for generation to finish and check that both signs are visible. This adaptation explicitly starts with ordinary surface shading when reusing an instance. Opening a document can retain a session’s X-ray or clipping shader; clearing it makes the two phase colors visible before you add the X-ray finish in step 6. The colors show the sign of orbital amplitude , not positive and negative electric charge. Squaring an orbital removes that sign. A surface encloses a chosen amplitude level; it is not a hard boundary of the electron. 4. Compose the view Set the background to dark blue #10243a, enable ambient occlusion for the molecule, and rotate the current view 30 degrees horizontally and 15 degrees vertically. Confirm those changes without changing the orbital surfaces. Checkpoint: the background is dark blue, the atomic framework gains AO shading, and the camera turns from its fitted pose. The HOMO’s isovalue and mesh resolution remain unchanged. Ambient occlusion adds visual depth to the molecule. It is a display effect, independent of the orbital calculation and the field’s two phases. 5. Export opaque and transparent PNGs Save this view as homo.png in my output folder. Also export homo-transparent.png with a transparent background. Use fresh filenames if either exists. Show me both images here and tell me their dimensions and where they were saved. Checkpoint: both PNG files exist and open. The opaque image includes #10243a ; the transparent one has an alpha background while keeping the molecular and surface shading. The recorded exports are 1700 × 1328 pixels; your dimensions follow your actual viewport. Inspect the images, not just the filenames. Export captures the current view and does not save a molecular document. The visible background is restored after a transparent export. 6. Give the surfaces an X-ray finish Give both HOMO surfaces an X-ray finish: make their front-facing centers almost transparent and their contours strong and cyan. Use the built-in X-ray preset and adjust its available appearance controls. Keep the current viewing angle and dark blue background. Export a new homo-xray.png in my output folder and show it to me. Checkpoint: the framework is visible through the shell and its contours are more prominent. Both signed surfaces remain at the same isovalue and 64³ resolution; only their finish changes. A useful starting point is zero minimum opacity, 85% maximum opacity and a cutoff that removes opacity below 3%. These are suggested appearance settings; the recording did not preserve its exact numeric adjustments. Ask the agent to inspect the result as it tunes them. This visual finish is not an X-ray simulation. 7. Round the contours Remember the exact current viewing angle and framing. Increase the HOMO mesh grid resolution from 64 to 128, keeping the same ±0.03 isosurfaces. Wait for the new surfaces to finish and tell me their triangle count. Restore the previous angle and framing afterward, and check that they match the preceding image. Keep the same X-ray finish and background. Export a new homo-xray-128.png in my output folder and show me the result. Checkpoint: the surfaces have smoother contours at 128³, with the preceding view restored and the X-ray settings unchanged. The recorded final result has 18,736 triangles . Compare the settings and actual image if your result differs; a larger grid improves spatial sampling without changing the supplied wavefunction. Regenerating geometry can change the framing automatically. Asking the agent to remember and restore the view keeps the before-and-after comparison useful. The isovalue 0.03 specifies the magnitude for both orbital signs. Refining this orbital replaces its saved meshes. Keep a separate molecular document if you want both resolutions. Keep exploring To retain the scientific data and generated geometry, ask the agent to save a new .eigenvista file in your output folder. Viewing angle, shader appearance, AO and background are session settings, so keep your prompts and PNGs to reproduce the appearance. The density lesson explains what is saved and compares direct sampled rendering with mesh-based cutaways. If a calculation is slow, use the cancellation prompt . Starting a calculation is not the same as finishing it; ask the agent to check its progress before continuing. More AI lessons Density and interiors → Ambient occlusion → Molecular representations →

title: Look inside electron density
description: Ask an external AI agent to discover occupation-derived density, compare volume and raycast previews, generate a mesh, reveal its interior and save the molecular document.
text: Move from a signed orbital to a density envelope. Explore the sampled field first, then make geometry you can shade, cut open and save. Use the same real calculation Complete AI connection setup and read the external-agent guide . This lesson uses the connection tools included in the EigenVista 0.8.0 Mac app . Give the prompts to your external Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode or other local agent; there is no embedded EigenVista chat box. Use the included bicyclic-c7h10.molden , the same 17-atom C 7 H 10 example as the recorded orbital lesson . Your agent can also download it into the input folder. Use the connected window and folders chosen during setup. Keep the original input and use new filenames for your results. Here density is the occupation-weighted sum of squared listed orbitals: ρ(r) = Σ n i |ψ i (r)|². It is nonnegative and has units of electrons/bohr³. It has no positive/negative orbital phase. The importer cannot recover omitted orbitals or core electrons, and the source does not identify its calculation method. This is an occupation-derived density, not a new SCF calculation or an independently supplied correlated density. 1. Discover the density by its meaning Use our connected EigenVista window. Save any unsaved work to a new .eigenvista file in my output folder before opening another document; do not discard it. Open bicyclic-c7h10.molden from my examples folder. Find the total electron density derived from the listed orbital occupations, checking its scientific meaning rather than just its name. Tell me its units and the atom, basis-function and orbital counts. Remove any previous X-ray or clipping effect. Checkpoint: the document has 17 atoms, 125 basis functions and 118 orbitals. The density is described as occupation-derived, with units of electrons/bohr³. Its label may simply say “Occupation-derived density (listed orbitals)”. An imported cube with unspecified scalar meaning is unsuitable for this lesson: its filename cannot establish that it contains electron density. 2. Explore a volume without generating meshes Show that total density as a volume preview at grid resolution 48 and isovalue 0.04 electrons/bohr³. Use #93e8d9 for the density, 100% opacity and a #17232d background. Show the molecule as ball and stick. Wait until the preview finishes, then fit it in the view. Confirm that no surface meshes were created. Export density-volume-48.png in my output folder and show me the image. Checkpoint: a volume preview appears at 48³ and no saved surfaces have been created. The density is sampled directly for rendering. At this stage an image exists, but there is no new mesh geometry to save. The 0.04 electrons/bohr³ value controls how the field is displayed. Volume opacity accumulates samples along viewing rays; the result is not a sharp physical skin around a molecule. 3. Compare a sampled raycast Remember the current viewing angle and framing. Keep the same density, 0.04 isovalue and colors, but switch to a sampled raycast preview at grid resolution 64. Wait until it finishes, then restore the same angle and framing for comparison. Confirm that there are still no saved surface meshes. Export density-raycast-64.png in my output folder, show it beside the volume image and explain what changed. Checkpoint: the raycast preview uses a 64³ grid and the saved-surface count stays zero. The apparent boundary is rendered from sampled values; neither preview creates mesh geometry. Because this step also increases spatial resolution, use the same resolution for both modes if you want to compare only the rendering method. Sampling quality is a separate display choice: it changes samples along rays, while grid resolution changes samples in space. Neither creates additional quantum-chemistry input data. 4. Keep a density surface Remember the current viewing angle and framing. Generate a surface mesh for this density at isovalue 0.04 electrons/bohr³ and grid resolution 128. Wait until it is finished, then tell me the isovalue, grid resolution and triangle count. Restore the previous angle and framing after generation, check that they match the preview and show me the completed surface. Checkpoint: a saved positive density surface now appears at 0.04 electrons/bohr³, generated on a 128³ grid. The view matches the preceding preview after the agent restores it. There is no negative-phase partner for this nonnegative total density. A mesh is an extracted constant-density surface. It can be retained in the native file and given a surface shader; the direct sampled previews did not create this geometry. 5. See the framework through the shell Give the density surface an X-ray finish so I can see the framework through it. Use the built-in X-ray preset with transparency enabled, zero minimum opacity, 85% maximum opacity and a cutoff that removes opacity below 3%. Keep the same viewing angle and background. Export density-xray-128.png in my output folder and show me the image. Checkpoint: the density geometry and triangle count are unchanged, while front-facing areas become more transparent and the outline stays stronger. The shader is an appearance effect on a mesh; the density values are unchanged. A separate real GUI capture of this example’s occupation-derived total density at 0.04 electrons/bohr³ on a 256³ mesh. It illustrates the finish; its resolution and camera differ from this 128³ agent workflow. 6. Cut a window into the density Replace the X-ray finish with the built-in surface-clipping preset and make the remaining shell opaque. Keep the clipping coordinate scale at 0.24. Set the clipping box to -10 through 10 on each axis, then lower its upper z boundary to 0.25 to open a window. Rotate 35 degrees horizontally and 15 degrees vertically to inspect the opening. Export density-clipped-128.png and a transparent-background density-clipped-128-transparent.png in my output folder. Show me both. Checkpoint: a clipping plane exposes the molecular framework inside the envelope. The saved mesh and scientific field still have the same counts and values: the shader hides fragments rather than cutting atoms or rewriting geometry. The exported transparent background is independent of the surface shader’s own transparency setting. The same clipping parameters on a 256³ density mesh in a separate GUI capture. Its oblique camera was chosen interactively to show the opening; it is not a screenshot of the 128³ prompt sequence. Keep the clipping coordinate scale fixed while moving a boundary. To look from the other side, ask the agent to rotate the view; to restore the complete shell, remove the clipping effect. 7. Save data and preserve the view Save the current molecular document as c7h10-density.eigenvista in my output folder, using another fresh name if it exists. Confirm that the file was saved successfully and contains our latest work. Tell me what it retains. Record the current view, surface finish and appearance settings, ambient occlusion and background in your response so I can recreate this image later. Leave EigenVista running. Checkpoint: the new molecular file exists and contains your latest work. It retains molecular data, basis/orbitals, the occupation-derived density, provenance, generated mesh and its generation settings. Global representation, surface colors, opacity and saved-mesh visibility are also document appearance. Viewing angle, surface finish, AO and background are session settings. They are not stored in .eigenvista . Sampled orbital/density previews must also be prepared again after reopening. Keep the recorded prompts/settings and PNGs with the molecular file; reapply the appearance to recreate the view. See what is saved . Follow progress and stop a calculation Starting a calculation does not mean it has finished. Ask the agent to wait for the completed result before judging an image or moving to the next step. Live percentages describe the current phase, not the whole calculation. If the agent stops waiting, the app may still be working; ask it to check progress again. If a preview or mesh step is taking longer than you want, give this prompt while that work is active: Check the density calculation I just requested. If it is still waiting or running, cancel only that calculation and wait until the app is ready again. Keep every previously completed surface. Tell me whether it was cancelled or had already finished. If it already finished, leave its result in place. Checkpoint: the calculation has stopped and the app is ready again. Completed geometry from earlier steps remains. If the calculation finished before cancellation, its result stays in place. Ask for a lower grid resolution if you want a quicker retry. More AI lessons Recorded orbital session → Ambient occlusion → Molecular representations →

title: Read crowded molecules with AO
description: Ask an external agent to compare atomic representations and matched-camera ambient-occlusion images of the 58,870-atom 1AON complex in EigenVista.
text: Turn a crowded atomic view into a readable study of molecular packing. Ask your agent to compare three representations, add matte ambient occlusion, and keep a pair of images from exactly the same camera. Get ready Complete external-agent setup and read the AI control guide first. Give the prompts to Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, or another connected local agent that can inspect images. The connection tools are included in the EigenVista 0.8.0 Mac app . The agent can download 1AON.cif into your input folder and use the included MatterViz Pastel palette. If you already have those files, give it their locations. The palette is also available as matterviz-pastel.json . Keep original inputs and choose new output names for repeated runs. The input is the deposited GroEL–GroES chaperonin complex, RCSB PDB 1AON . EigenVista imports 58,870 selected atoms . The goal is two comparison PNGs, a closer finished view, and a native molecular document. 1. Open the complex Copy this into your external agent after supplying the approved file locations from setup: Use my connected EigenVista instance and only the input and output directories I approved. If the current molecule has unsaved work, save it under a new name before replacing it; never discard it silently. Open 1AON.cif. If I do not already have it, download https://uvar-apps.github.io/eigenvista/downloads/1AON.cif into my input folder first. Tell me how many atoms and chains were imported, which kinds of biological components are present, and whether the secondary-structure assignments came from the deposited file. Check for 58,870 selected atoms and summarize any import warnings before changing the view. Checkpoint: the agent reports 58,870 atoms and the imported biological identities, preserving any earlier work. Let import and scene preparation finish before judging the picture. 2. Give the atoms a lighter palette MatterViz Pastel is recommended for AO: its light element colors leave room for shaded contacts and cavities. Ask the agent to load the downloaded palette and prepare a complete atomic view. Load the included matterviz-pastel.json palette and color the structure by element. Show the complete complex, removing any earlier chain or component filters and special representation choices. Use Ball and stick for the whole structure, turn ambient occlusion off, choose automatic AO radius, and set the background to #ecebe4. Fit the whole complex in the view. Confirm that MatterViz Pastel is active and show me a PNG so I can check the lighter element colors. Checkpoint: the full complex is framed and its atom colors use Pastel. Chain, entity and secondary-structure coloring serve different tasks; Element coloring displays the palette’s element colors. 3. Choose the atomic representation Representation Use it to read Ball and stick Atomic positions and connectivity; a dense whole-complex view can be visually busy. Liquorice The connected atomic framework with a more uniform stick-like appearance. Van der Waals Space-filling atomic envelopes, packing and broad recesses; bond cylinders are hidden. Keep the camera, background and palette fixed, with ambient occlusion off. Compare Ball and stick, Liquorice and Van der Waals in that order. Save a new PNG of each in my approved output directory and show me the actual images. Wait for each view to finish preparing before taking its picture. Explain what each representation reveals about this crowded complex, then leave Van der Waals selected. Preserve the imported atoms and connectivity. Checkpoint: three images show different depictions of the same complex. Van der Waals has atomic spheres without bond cylinders; hiding those cylinders does not remove connectivity from the document. 4. Compare AO off and on from one camera Choose a view with both outer contacts and a broad recess visible. The agent can orbit and zoom before the pair, but must keep the camera fixed between captures. With Van der Waals selected, fit the complete structure, rotate the view 25 degrees horizontally and 10 degrees vertically, and zoom in by a factor of 1.08. Keep that exact camera angle and framing for the comparison. Save a new 1aon-ao-off.png with ambient occlusion off. Then enable ambient occlusion at 100% strength with automatic radius and save a new 1aon-ao-on.png. Wait for each image to finish, then show them side by side. Keep the representation, palette, background and image dimensions unchanged. Confirm that the camera matches and tell me the radius used. Reference capture: normal molecular material, AO off, MatterViz Pastel, Element coloring, Van der Waals spheres and background #ecebe4 . The next image uses the same camera and geometry. These existing reference captures used a palette loaded through the GUI. Reference capture: AO on at 100% strength with automatic radius. Active AO uses Lambert shading plus SSAO, without specular highlights. The comparison includes the matte material change as well as the occlusion effect. Checkpoint: the two exported views have matching framing and element colors, while AO emphasizes contacts and recesses. Off, or zero strength, restores the normal molecular material. The reference images illustrate the result; your chosen orbit need not reproduce their exact angle. AO shades atomic spheres and bonds only . Protein ribbons, cartoons and custom field surfaces keep their own materials. It is an approximate screen-space depth cue, so visible shading can change with the camera and cannot account for all hidden or offscreen geometry. 5. Tune the scale, then move closer Automatic radius comes from the atom-coordinate extent and stays fixed as you zoom. Compare a gentler strength and a smaller neighborhood before moving the camera. Keep the comparison camera fixed. Lower AO strength to 60%, save a new comparison PNG, and show it beside the 100% image. Then use 100% strength with a manual radius of 8 angstroms. Save another PNG and explain how the scale of the shading changes. Return to automatic radius. Rotate a further 15 degrees horizontally and zoom in by a factor of 1.15 to explore a recess. Show me a new image and explain which broad features remain readable. If the model is clipped, zoom out without changing its molecular data. Checkpoint: changing radius adjusts the scale of the shading, while camera movement changes its screen-space appearance. Manual radius supports 0.25–50 Å. The final view uses automatic radius again. If navigation is slow, ask the agent to turn AO off while you explore. 6. Keep the view and the molecular data Keep this Van der Waals view, the Pastel palette and the current AO settings. Save two new final PNGs in my approved output directory: one with the current background and one with a transparent background. Show me both, check that the transparent one has an alpha background, and report their filenames and dimensions. Save a new molecular document named 1aon-packing.eigenvista without overwriting anything. Record the camera, background, palette, Element coloring and AO settings in your reply so I can recreate this appearance later. Checkpoint: you have the comparison images, two finished PNGs, and a new native file. The native document retains the selected molecular data, biological identities, connectivity and global representation. AO, palette, background, biological display choices and camera are session settings; Save does not preserve them. A PNG preserves the rendered appearance. If a save or image export fails, ask the agent to check the destination before retrying and use fresh names for existing files. An AO enhancement error leaves normal molecular rendering available; ask the agent to disable and re-enable AO before trying again. Sources and next steps Structure and original scientific citation: RCSB PDB 1AON . The palette preserves Janosh Riebesell’s MatterViz colors for elements 1–109; see the MIT notice . Download sources and reuse notes and the image provenance record accompany the examples. Continue with your agent Read the assembly with protein views → Explore frontier orbitals → Shape a density surface →

title: Read a large protein assembly
description: Use natural-language prompts to compare four protein representations of 1AON, distinguish chains and entities, and focus on one protein chain.
text: Step back from atomic packing to see how a large complex is organized. Ask your agent to compare backbone traces, smooth tubes, ribbons and cartoons, then study the deposited fold of one chain. Get ready Complete external-agent setup and read the AI control guide . The connection tools are included in the EigenVista 0.8.0 Mac app . Give the prompts to your connected Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, or another local agent with an image viewer. Use 1AON.cif again, this time to study the GroEL–GroES assembly rather than its crowded atomic envelope. Give your agent the file location and the folder where you want the pictures saved, using the connection established during setup. Keep original inputs and use new output names for repeated runs. Outcome: four protein-view PNGs, a chain-colored assembly overview, and a focused chain illustration. 1. Inspect the structure before choosing a view Use my connected EigenVista instance. If 1AON.cif is already open, continue with it. Otherwise save any unsaved work under a new name before opening 1AON.cif. If needed, download https://uvar-apps.github.io/eigenvista/downloads/1AON.cif into my input folder first. Never discard existing work silently. Tell me the imported atom and chain counts, the kinds of biological components present, and whether the secondary-structure assignments came from the deposited file. Expect 58,870 selected atoms. Show the complete structure, removing earlier visibility filters and special chain or component representation choices. Turn ambient occlusion off, use Element coloring and set the background to #ecebe4. Checkpoint: the full imported complex is available for comparison and the agent reports its biological identities. Keep one coloring choice throughout the four-view comparison. Choose the level of detail Global representation Useful question Ball and stick Where are the atoms and their connections? Liquorice How does the connected atomic framework run through this region? Van der Waals How tightly do atomic envelopes pack? Try the AO lesson . Backbone trace How do the protein backbone paths arrange themselves across the assembly? Smooth tube How do those paths flow through space when drawn as rounded tubes? Ribbon How do the oriented protein ribbons fold within each subunit? Secondary-structure cartoon Where do deposited helices, strand arrows and connecting loops organize the fold? The first three modes depict atoms. The four protein modes draw the backbone while nonprotein components retain atomic detail. Missing backbone atoms, chain ends and unsupported gaps break paths; the viewer does not draw invented connections. Missing secondary assignments remain thin gray unassigned loops in ribbon/cartoon views. 2. Follow the backbone with trace and tube Show the complete assembly as a Backbone trace. Wait for the view to finish preparing, fit the whole complex, then rotate 25 degrees horizontally and 10 degrees vertically. Keep this exact camera angle and framing for all four protein views. Save and show me a new 1aon-trace.png. Change only the representation to Smooth tube, wait for it to finish preparing, then save and show me a new 1aon-tube.png. Compare the backbone paths and rounded tubes at matching framing. Checkpoint: trace and tube follow the same protein paths, with different thickness and shape. Atom and chain counts remain unchanged. On this large input, wait for protein geometry to finish preparing before judging a blank or old view. 3. Compare ribbons and secondary-structure cartoons Keep the same assembly camera, background, colors and visible components. Show Ribbon, wait for it to finish preparing, then save and show me a new 1aon-ribbon.png. Repeat with Secondary-structure cartoon and save 1aon-cartoon.png. Compare how ribbons, helical regions, strand arrows and connecting loops reveal the folds. Explain which assignments were supplied by the deposited structure. Describe missing or unassigned regions as unknown, without predicting secondary structure. Leave the cartoon view selected. Reference capture: the full 1AON complex in protein cartoons with Chain coloring. This existing image was made with the GUI; the next step asks your agent to choose the biological colors. Protein depiction geometry uses its own diffuse shading, outside molecular AO. Checkpoint: you have four distinct protein-view images of one assembly. Unknown secondary structure remains explicit even with chain or entity coloring. If carbonyl orientation is unavailable, the app can show a thin tube with an informational notice; isolated backbone points remain markers. 4. Distinguish chains and entities Chain coloring separates deposited chain instances. Entity coloring groups chains that belong to the same supplied molecular entity. Their legends identify the colors; color alone does not establish identity. Keep the complete assembly in the cartoon representation and keep the camera fixed. Color it by Chain, save a new 1aon-chains.png and show me the image. Then color it by Entity, save a new 1aon-entities.png and show me that image too. Explain how chain instances differ from molecular entities in this deposited structure, using the imported identities and the images. Preserve the molecule and the four earlier comparison views. Checkpoint: chain colors distinguish subunits, while chains sharing an entity receive the same entity color. The complete molecular data remain unchanged. 5. Focus on one deposited fold Find protein chain A using the deposited chain identities. Isolate it and frame that visible chain closely. Keep the cartoon representation, and color it by the deposited secondary structure. Save and show me a new 1aon-chain-a.png. Point out helices, strand arrows and unassigned connecting regions in the actual image. Keep unknown assignments explicit, and confirm that the other chains are hidden rather than removed from the molecular document. Reference capture: chain A isolated and focused, with deposited secondary-structure coloring. This existing image was made with the GUI. Isolation hides other chains without removing their molecular data. Checkpoint: one protein chain fills the view. Assigned helices and strands are distinct from gray unassigned regions. EigenVista uses deposited annotations; it does not run DSSP or predict missing assignments. 6. Finish the overview and keep the result Restore the complete structure and remove any chain or component representation choices that would override the whole-assembly view. Use Secondary-structure cartoon for the protein, color by Chain, and frame the entire complex. Choose a readable overview with rotation and zoom, and show me a candidate image before the final export. Save new opaque and transparent overview PNGs in my approved output directory. Show me both images and report their filenames and dimensions. Save a new 1aon-assembly.eigenvista without overwriting anything. Record the camera, representation, coloring and other display choices so I can recreate this presentation. Checkpoint: the overview shows the whole complex and the focused-chain PNG shows the chosen subunit. Save retains molecular data, biological identities, connectivity and the global representation. Biological coloring, visibility, isolation, residue ranges, per-chain/component styles, focus, camera, background and palette are session choices; record them with the images if you want to reproduce the presentation. The atomic-packing lesson shows the complementary Ball and stick, Liquorice and Van der Waals views with MatterViz Pastel . AO shades atomic spheres and bonds, not the protein ribbons or custom field surfaces. Sources and next steps Structure and original scientific citation: RCSB PDB 1AON . Keep the download sources and reuse notes with redistributed inputs; the image provenance record documents the real application captures. The biological structure reference covers component filters, residue ranges and identity labels. More external-agent lessons Read atomic packing with AO → Explore frontier orbitals → Shape a density surface →

title: About EigenVista
description: EigenVista's origins in Ugo Varetto's 2006–2010 Molekel project, plus its design, author, data credits and project links.
text: The purpose History Author and copyright Cite EigenVista Local by design Current boundaries Credits The project A viewer for molecular data EigenVista brings atomic structures, imported orbitals, density data and sampled scalar fields into one interactive scene. The aim is to help you inspect supplied scientific data and prepare useful views of it. From Molekel to EigenVista EigenVista is a modern rewrite of Molekel , the molecular visualization application developed by Ugo Varetto from 2006 to 2010 . Molekel brought together molecular structures, quantum chemistry surfaces and programmable shaders. EigenVista carries that project forward with a new implementation and name. Machine-readable citation metadata ↗ Local by design The desktop application reads and processes local files on your computer. Its scientific core is written in Rust; the interface uses React and Three.js/WebGL2, inside a Tauri desktop shell. Scientific field work runs in a background WebAssembly worker, keeping progress and cancellation available. There is no calculation server or account required for local molecular-file workflows. This website provides documentation, examples and downloads; it does not upload or analyze your calculation files. A native document can hold structure, supplied quantum data, sampled fields and generated meshes together. New documents use .eigenvista; older .molekel preview documents remain readable. Display choices such as the background, palette and AO remain session preferences. See the file reference for what is saved. Know what a view means Imported fields retain their declared meaning. Unknown cube units or scalar meaning are not guessed. Protein secondary structure uses deposited annotations. AO uses screen-space shading to emphasize depth and contact regions. Display bonds are inferred or taken from supported declarations. They do not establish bond order, crystallographic symmetry or a complete chemical interpretation. Version 0.8.0 is an experimental development preview. The downloadable package targets Apple Silicon Macs; Linux, Windows, Intel Mac and the full deployment-OS range are not qualified distributions. Preserve original calculation files and inspect import reports. Images, examples and palettes The molecular images were captured in EigenVista from the repository's public test inputs. The large-structure studies use PDB 1AON and PDB 4PJ1 . See each RCSB entry for the deposited structure and its original scientific citation. The quantum and shader studies use the C₇H₁₀ Molden example , originally distributed with Molekel . See the dataset notes for the source and orbital information. The 29-atom cube study uses complex-field.cube , originally elf_pic.cube in the same Molekel example collection. The small water Molden example remains available as a separate RHF/cc-pVDZ input. Water PDB/XYZ coordinates and the signed-affine cube are demonstration fixtures; the cube is a mathematical signed field, not a quantum calculation. Example sources and notices and the capture record preserve provenance and settings. MatterViz Muted and Pastel are adaptations of Janosh Riebesell's MatterViz element colors . Original RGB values for elements 1–109 are retained; remaining elements use EigenVista defaults. The MIT notice accompanies both palettes. Download Pastel for the recommended AO workflow.
